etymology: Webster (1828) enters DESPOTISM without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines despotism as “absolute power; authority unlimited and uncontrolled by men, constitution or laws, and depending alone on the will of the prince,” and as “an arbitrary government.” Scripture describes such power without approving it: “whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he set up; and whom he would he put down” (Dan 5:19). Rehoboam chose it: “My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke” (1Ki 12:14). God’s law forbade the king’s heart to be “lifted up above his brethren” (Deu 17:20). Only God holds power unlimited by any other, and He is just.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DESPOTISM, absolute power unlimited by men, constitution or laws, depending on the will of the prince; an arbitrary government.
webster_full: DESPOTISM, noun
1. Absolute power; authority unlimited and uncontrolled by men, constitution or laws, and depending alone on the will of the prince; as the despotism of a Turkish sultan.
2. An arbitrary government, as that of Turkey and Persia.
scriptures: Dan 5:19

And for the majesty that he gave him, all people, nations, and languages, trembled and feared before him: whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive; and whom he would he set up; and whom he would he put down.
Dan 5:20
But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:

And spake to them after the counsel of the young men, saying, My father made your yoke heavy, and I will add to your yoke: my father also chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.

That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left: to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel.
corruption_summary: Despotism is now used loosely for any strict rule; Webster meant power that no law or constitution limits.
corruption_paragraphs: The heart of Webster’s definition is “uncontrolled by men, constitution or laws.” A strict but lawful ruler is not a despot; a pleasant ruler who answers to no law is one.
Nebuchadnezzar’s absolute power ended when “his heart was lifted up” and God humbled him (Dan 5:19–20). Scripture keeps every ruler under a higher law.
roots_summary: Power that answers to no law, depending only on the ruler’s will.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): absolute power; authority unlimited and uncontrolled.
Webster: depending alone on the will of the prince.
Whom he would he slew (Dan 5:19).
I will add to your yoke (1Ki 12:14).

etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr. rule.] The Greek letters are not printed in the live text.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines anarchy as “want of government; a state of society, when there is no law or supreme power, or when the laws are not efficient, and individuals do what they please with impunity; political confusion.” Judges closes on exactly that state: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Jdg 21:25). Isaiah names its fruit: “the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient, and the base against the honourable” (Isa 3:5). Order is from God, “for God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33), and “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ANARCHY, want of government; no law or supreme power, or laws not efficient, so that individuals do what they please with impunity; political confusion.
webster_full: AN'ARCHY, noun [Gr. rule.]
Want of government; a state of society, when there is no law or supreme power, or when the laws are not efficient, and individuals do what they please with impunity; political confusion.
scriptures: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Isa 3:5
And the people shall be oppressed, every one by another, and every one by his neighbour: the child shall behave himself proudly against the ancient, and the base against the honourable.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
corruption_summary: Anarchy is now sometimes praised as freedom from rule; Webster called it confusion where men do what they please with impunity.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster saw anarchy not only where there is no law but “when the laws are not efficient.” Laws left unenforced bring the same state.
Modern use romanticizes the word as a creed of liberty. Scripture shows its end: every man right in his own eyes, and the weak oppressed (Jdg 21:25; Isa 3:5).
roots_summary: Without rule: no law, or laws not enforced, and every man his own judge.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): want of government.
Webster: individuals do what they please with impunity.
Every man did that which was right in his own eyes (Jdg 21:25).
God is not the author of confusion (1Co 14:33).

pos: n. (the office of a magistrate; the body of magistrates)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines magistracy as “the office or dignity of a magistrate” and “the body of magistrates.” His illustration is pointed: “Duelling is not only an usurpation of the divine prerogative, but it is an insult upon magistracy.” Private vengeance usurps an office God gave the magistrate. Paul says the ruler “is the minister of God to thee for good” and “a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). Believers are told “to obey magistrates” (Tit 3:1), and rulers are sent “for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well” (1Pe 2:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): MAGISTRACY, the office or dignity of a magistrate; the body of magistrates.
webster_full: MAG'ISTRACY, adjective [See Magistrate.] The office or dignity of a magistrate.
Duelling is not only an usurpation of the divine prerogative, but it is an insult upon magistracy
1. The body of magistrates.
scriptures: Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Tit 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
Or unto governors, as unto them that are sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, and for the praise of them that do well.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Magistracy has faded from speech; the idea of civil office as a ministry under God has faded with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s example joins two offences: duelling usurps God’s prerogative and insults the magistracy. Both assume that civil judgment is a trust from God.
Modern speech treats office as a job or a prize. Scripture calls the magistrate God’s minister for good and the sword-bearer against evil (Rom 13:4).
roots_summary: The office of the civil ruler, held as God’s minister.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): the office or dignity of a magistrate.
Webster: duelling is an insult upon magistracy.
He is the minister of God to thee for good (Rom 13:4).
Obey magistrates (Tit 3:1).
usage: The office or dignity of a magistrate

pos: n. (sworn men who try matters of fact)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a jury as “a number of freeholders, selected in the manner prescribed by law, empaneled and sworn to inquire into and try any matter of fact, and to declare the truth on the evidence given them in the case.” The root is the oath: the jury is sworn. Scripture binds every judge to the truth and to evidence. “At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is worthy of death be put to death” (Deu 17:6). “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exo 23:2). And a hearing must hear both sides: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JURY, freeholders selected by law, sworn to try matters of fact and declare the truth on the evidence; grand and petty juries; the decision of a petty jury is a verdict.
webster_full: JU'RY, noun [Latin juro, to swear.] A number of freeholders, selected in the manner prescribed by law, empaneled and sworn to inquire into and try any matter of fact, and to declare the truth on the evidence given them in the case. Grand juries consist usually of twenty four freeholders at least, and are summoned to try matters alleged in indictments. Petty juries, consisting usually of twelve men, attend courts to try matters of fact in civil causes, and to decide both the law and the fact in criminal prosecutions. The decision of a petty jury is called a verdict.
scriptures: Deu 17:6
At the mouth of two witnesses, or three witnesses, shall he that is worthy of death be put to death; but at the mouth of one witness he shall not be put to death.
Exo 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
And the judges shall make diligent inquisition: and, behold, if the witness be a false witness, and hath testified falsely against his brother;
corruption_summary: The jury is now often thought of as a panel of opinion; Webster’s jury is sworn to declare the truth on the evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s jurors are sworn (Latin juro) and bound to “declare the truth on the evidence given them.” Verdicts given from sympathy, pressure or the mood of the crowd break that oath.
Exodus forbids a judge to follow a multitude to do evil (Exo 23:2). The oath before God is what makes twelve men a jury.
roots_summary: Latin, to swear: men under oath who declare the truth on the evidence.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): empaneled and sworn to inquire into and try any matter of fact.
Webster: to declare the truth on the evidence.
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil (Exo 23:2).
His neighbour cometh and searcheth him (Pro 18:17).
usage: The decision of a petty jury is called a verdict

pos: n. (a privilege or right granted; liberty)
etymology: Webster (1828): [See Frank.] He gives the root sense as “liberty, freedom.”
biblical_def: Webster (1828) says franchise is “properly, liberty, freedom,” and hence “a particular privilege or right granted by a prince or sovereign to an individual or to a number of persons.” His example: “the right to vote for governor, senators and representatives, is a franchise belonging to citizens, and not enjoyed by aliens.” Paul used his civil franchise in Roman courts; the chief captain said, “With a great sum obtained I this freedom,” and Paul answered, “But I was free born” (Act 22:28). Israel’s jubilee was a public grant of liberty: “proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” (Lev 25:10). The highest franchise is Christ’s: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (Gal 5:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FRANCHISE, properly liberty; a privilege or right granted by a sovereign, as the vote belonging to citizens; exemption from a burden; the district of an immunity.
webster_full: FRAN'CHISE, noun fran'chiz. [See Frank.] Properly, liberty, freedom. Hence,

1. A particular privilege or right granted by a prince or sovereign to an individual or to a number of persons; as the right to be a body corporate with perpetual succession; the right to hold a court leet or other court; to have waifs, wrecks, treasure-treve, or forfeitures. So the right to vote for governor, senators and representatives, is a franchise belonging to citizens, and not enjoyed by aliens. The right to establish a bank, is a franchise
2. Exemption from a burden or duty to which others are subject.
3. The district or jurisdiction to which a particular privilege extends; the limits of an immunity.
4. An asylum or sanctuary, where persons are secure from arrest.
Churches and monasteries in Spain are franchises for criminals.
FRAN'CHISE, verb transitive To make free; but enfranchise is more generally used.
scriptures: And the chief captain answered, With a great sum obtained I this freedom. And Paul said, But I was free born.

And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you; and ye shall return every man unto his possession, and ye shall return every man unto his family.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
And as they bound him with thongs, Paul said unto the centurion that stood by, Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?
corruption_summary: Franchise now means chiefly a licensed brand of store or a sports team; Webster’s liberty and civil right are secondary.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster began with liberty and moved to granted rights, including the vote. Modern business use (a restaurant franchise) has nearly taken over the word.
A franchise is a trust granted, not a thing made by the holder. Paul used his citizenship for the gospel’s sake (Act 22:25–28).
roots_summary: Root sense liberty; a right granted, such as the citizen’s vote.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): properly, liberty, freedom.
Webster: the right to vote is a franchise belonging to citizens.
But I was free born (Act 22:28).
Proclaim liberty throughout all the land (Lev 25:10).
usage: Exemption from a burden or duty to which others are subject

pos: n. (a written instrument of a grant)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters CHARTER without an etymology note in the live text; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a charter as “a written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.” In its usual sense it is “the instrument of a grant conferring powers, rights and privileges.” He notes that “the charters under which most of the colonies in America were settled, were given by the king of England.” Scripture records such instruments. Cyrus’s decree let the Jews go up to build (Ezr 1:3). Nehemiah asked for “a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest” for timber (Neh 2:8). A sealed royal writing could not be reversed (Est 8:8). God’s own grants are covenants, sealed by His word.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CHARTER, a written instrument given as evidence of a grant or contract; the instrument conferring powers, rights and privileges, as the colonial charters.
webster_full: CHARTER, noun

1. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man. In its more usual sense, it is the instrument of a grant conferring powers, rights and privileges, either from a king or other sovereign power, or from a private person, as a charter of exemption, that no person shall be empannelled on a jury, a charter of pardon, etc. The charters under which most of the colonies in America were settled, were given by the king of England, and incorporated certain persons, with powers to hold the lands granted, to establish a government, and make laws for their own regulation. These were called charter-governments.
2. Any instrument, executed with form and solemnity, bestowing rights or privileges.
3. Privilege; immunity; exemption.
My mother, Who has a charter to extol her blood, When she does praise me, grieves me.
CHARTER, verb transitive
1. To hire or to let a ship by charter [See Charter-party.]
2. To establish by charter
scriptures: Ezr 1:3

Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the LORD God of Israel, (he is the God,) which is in Jerusalem.
Neh 2:8

And a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the palace which appertained to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall enter into. And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.
Est 8:8

Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse.
Gen 17:7
And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee.
corruption_summary: Charter now often means a hired bus or boat, or a school’s legal form; Webster’s written grant of rights is pushed aside.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s charter is evidence in writing of what was granted. Modern use drifts to renting a vehicle or to mission statements called charters that grant nothing.
Scripture’s sealed writings carried real authority (Est 8:8; Neh 2:8). A charter binds because it is written and attested.
roots_summary: A written grant: powers, rights and privileges set down and attested.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a written instrument given as evidence of a grant.
Webster: conferring powers, rights and privileges.
A letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king’s forest (Neh 2:8).
The king’s sealed writing may no man reverse (Est 8:8).
usage: the instrument of a grant conferring powers, rights and privileges

pos: n. (the body invested with power to make laws)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters LEG’ISLATURE without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a legislature as “the body of men in a state or kingdom, invested with power to make and repeal laws; the supreme power of a state.” He notes that “the legislatures of most of the states in America, consist of two houses or branches.” Scripture sets one Lawgiver above all such bodies: “the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isa 33:22); “There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy” (Jas 4:12). Human lawmakers are judged by His law: “Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees” (Isa 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): LEGISLATURE, the body of men invested with power to make and repeal laws; the supreme power of a state; in America mostly of two houses.
webster_full: LEG'ISLATURE, noun the body of men in a state or kingdom, invested with power to make and repeal laws; the supreme power of a state. The legislature of Great Britain consists of the house of lords and the house of commons with the king, whose sanction is necessary to every bill before it becomes a law. The legislatures of most of the states in America, consist of two houses or branches, but the sanction of the govenor is required to give their acts the force of law, or a concurrence of two thirds of the two houses, after he has declined and assigned his objections.
scriptures: For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us.
Jas 4:12
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?
Isa 10:1
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
corruption_summary: A legislature is now often assumed to be the final source of right; Scripture places it under one Lawgiver.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster called the legislature “the supreme power of a state,” meaning supreme among men. Modern thought can treat whatever it enacts as right because it was enacted.
Isaiah’s woe is on those who write grievousness into law (Isa 10:1). Psalm 94 speaks of a throne “which frameth mischief by a law” (Psa 94:20).
roots_summary: The lawmaking body of a state, answerable to the one Lawgiver.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): invested with power to make and repeal laws.
Webster: most American legislatures consist of two houses.
The LORD is our lawgiver (Isa 33:22).
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees (Isa 10:1).
usage: invested with power to make and repeal laws
the supreme power of a state

pos: n. (the branch of government that tries controversies)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines the judiciary as “that branch of government which is concerned in the trial and determination of controversies between parties, and of criminal prosecutions; the system of courts of justice in a government.” He adds: “An independent judiciary is the firmest bulwark of freedom.” Moses was told, “Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates” (Deu 16:18), and those judges were charged, “thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift” (Deu 16:19). Jehoshaphat told his judges, “Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD” (2Ch 19:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JUDICIARY, the branch of government concerned in trying controversies and criminal prosecutions; the system of courts; an independent judiciary the firmest bulwark of freedom.
webster_full: JUDI'CIARY noun [Latin judiciarius.]
1. Passing judgment or sentence.
2. Pertaining to the courts of judicature or legal tribunals.

JUDI'CIARY, noun That branch of government which is concerned in the trial and determination of controversies between parties, and of criminal prosecutions; the system of courts of justice in a government. An independent judiciary is the firmest bulwark of freedom.
scriptures: Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the LORD thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.
Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.

And said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment.	[CACHE-ARTIFACT: verify no stray space-before-punct; pick another verse if it will not round-trip]

And let them judge the people at all seasons: and it shall be, that every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge: so shall it be easier for thyself, and they shall bear the burden with thee.
corruption_summary: The judiciary is now often expected to make policy; Webster’s judiciary tries and determines controversies.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s definition is about trial and determination. A court that writes policy has left that office.
His “independent judiciary” is independent of the other powers, not of God. Jehoshaphat’s judges judged “for the LORD” (2Ch 19:6).

pos: n. (a king-killer; the killing of a king)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin rex, king, and caedo, to slay.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines regicide as “A king-killer; one who murders a king,” and as “The killing or murder of a king.” David twice refused it when Saul was in his hand: “The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD’s anointed” (1Sa 24:6). When an Amalekite claimed to have killed Saul, David asked, “How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the LORD’s anointed?” (2Sa 1:14). The servants who slew Joash were later put to death by his son (2Ki 14:5). Scripture leaves the removal of kings to God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): REGICIDE, a king-killer; the killing or murder of a king.
webster_full: REG'ICIDE, noun [Latin rex, king, and caedo, to slay.]
1. A king-killer; one who murders a king.
2. The killing or murder of a king.
scriptures: And he said unto his men, The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD'S anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the LORD.
And David said unto him, How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the LORD'S anointed?
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD'S anointed, and be guiltless?
And it came to pass, as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand, that he slew his servants which had slain the king his father.
corruption_summary: Regicide is now a historical term, sometimes spoken of with admiration for those who killed tyrants; Webster calls it murder.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s definition uses the word “murders.” Modern histories can treat famous regicides as heroes and the word as neutral.
David’s restraint toward Saul, who was seeking his life, is Scripture’s example (1Sa 26:9). This entry does not settle every question of lawful resistance; it records the word and that example.
roots_summary: Latin king plus to slay: one who murders a king, or the deed.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a king-killer; one who murders a king.
Webster: the killing or murder of a king.
The LORD forbid that I should do this thing (1Sa 24:6).

pos: n. (one who loves and defends his country)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin patria, one’s native country, form pater, father.] (sic: “form” for “from” in the live text.)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a patriot as “a person who loves his country, and zealously supports and defends it and its interests.” The root is pater, father: the fatherland. The exile’s vow is patriot love: “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5). Nehemiah heard of Jerusalem’s ruin and “sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven” (Neh 1:4). Paul’s love for “my kinsmen according to the flesh” went deep (Rom 9:3). Even exiles were told, “seek the peace of the city” (Jer 29:7). The Christian’s first citizenship is in heaven (Php 3:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PATRIOT, a person who loves his country and zealously supports and defends it and its interests; as adjective, patriotic, as patriot zeal.
webster_full: PAT'RIOT, noun [Latin patria, one's native country, form pater, father.]
A person who loves his country, and zealously supports and defends it and its interests.
Such tears as patriots shed for dying laws.
PAT'RIOT, adjective Patriotic; devoted to the welfare of one's country; as patriot zeal.
scriptures: If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.
Neh 1:4
And it came to pass, when I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven,
Rom 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Jer 29:7
And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace.
Php 3:20
For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: Patriot is now used as a badge by rival factions; Webster’s love that supports and defends the country’s interests gets lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s patriot loves, supports and defends. Modern use often makes the word a label for one party, or a mark of suspicion.
Scripture’s patriots pray and weep for their people (Neh 1:4; Rom 9:3) and seek the good of the city where God puts them (Jer 29:7), while their final citizenship is in heaven (Php 3:20).
roots_summary: From pater, father: love of the fatherland that supports and defends it.
roots_lines: Webster (1828): a person who loves his country.
Webster: zealously supports and defends it and its interests.
